title: Courts (Civil and Criminal Justice) Reform Bill
what_it_is: Courts (Civil and Criminal Justice) Reform Bill

sections.label: Permanent remote hearing framework
sections.summary: A temporary remote hearing framework from April 2020 is to be replaced by a permanent framework facilitating technology in Court proceedings.

sentences.speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
sentences.text: In April 2020, we introduced a temporary remote hearing framework under the COVID-19 (Temporary Measures) Act to maintain access to justice amidst safe distancing measures.

sentences.speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
sentences.text: These measures have brought convenience to court users and also increased administrative efficiency.

sentences.speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
sentences.text: We are now looking to enact a permanent framework that will facilitate the use of technology in Court proceedings.

sections.label: Witness evidence by video-link
sections.summary: The Court may allow an expert witness or witness of fact to give evidence via video-link even if not in Singapore.

sentences.speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
sentences.text: First, the Court may now allow an expert witness or a witness of fact to give evidence via video-link even if the witness is not in Singapore.

sections.label: Accused appearing by video-link
sections.summary: The Court may allow an accused person to appear or give evidence via video-link from a stipulated location in Singapore.

sentences.speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
sentences.text: Second, the Court may allow an accused person to appear or give evidence via video-link from a stipulated location in Singapore, such as in Court or from a prison.

sections.label: AOJP Act consistency update
sections.summary: Part 2 of the Bill updates the AOJP Act to ensure consistency in how physical and remote court proceedings are treated.

sentences.speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
sentences.text: Part 2 of the Bill will update the AOJP Act to ensure consistency in the way physical and remote court proceedings are treated.

sections.label: Modernising Latin terms and jargon
sections.summary: The Bill modernises archaic Latin terms and technical legal jargon across more than 150 Acts, to simplify legal processes and enhance access to justice.

sentences.speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
sentences.text: This is part of the overall effort to simplify legal processes and also enhance access to justice.

sentences.speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
sentences.text: This Bill will modernise archaic Latin terms – terms which perhaps lawyers are most familiar with – and also technical legal jargon across more than 150 Acts.

sections.label: AG intervention statutory framework
sections.summary: Part 4 amends the Attorney-General (Additional Functions) Act to provide a statutory framework for the AG to intervene in court proceedings as guardian of the public interest.

sentences.speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
sentences.text: Part 4 of the Bill amends the Attorney-General (Additional Functions) Act to provide a statutory framework for the Attorney-General (AG) to intervene in court proceedings to fulfil his duty as guardian of the public interest.

sections.label: Interim relief for foreign proceedings
sections.summary: Part 5 amends the Civil Law Act to let the General Division of the High Court grant interim relief in aid of foreign court proceedings without substantive Singapore proceedings.

sentences.speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
sentences.text: Next, let me touch on Part 5 of the Bill which deals with freestanding interim relief.

sentences.speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
sentences.text: This Part amends the Civil Law Act to enable the General Division of the High Court to grant interim relief in aid of foreign court proceedings, even if there are no substantive proceedings in Singapore.

sections.label: Summary dismissal of appeals
sections.summary: The Bill amends the law to empower the General Division, State Courts and Family Courts to summarily dismiss appeals from lower Courts or the Registrar.

sentences.speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
sentences.text: The Bill will introduce amendments to empower the General Division, the State Courts and the Family Courts to also summarily dismiss appeals that arise from the lower Courts, or from a decision of the Registrar.

sections.label: Coram of three or more Judges
sections.summary: Clause 53 lets the Chief Justice convene a coram of three or more Judges to hear any civil or criminal matter before the General Division.

sentences.speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
sentences.text: Clause 53 of the Bill introduces amendments to allow the Chief Justice to convene a coram of three or more Judges to hear any civil or criminal matter before the General Division, if he considers appropriate.

sections.label: Arbitration proceedings heard in private
sections.summary: Clauses 8 and 30 amend the Arbitration Act and International Arbitration Act so proceedings under them are heard in private by default unless the Court orders open court.

sentences.speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
sentences.text: Given that these applications relate to arbitrations, such applications are often allowed by the Court.

sentences.speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
sentences.text: Hence, to better reflect the prevailing practice and streamline the process for parties, clauses 8 and 30 of the Bill will amend the Arbitration Act and the International Arbitration Act respectively, to provide that proceedings under these Acts are to be heard in private by default, unless the Court orders that the proceedings be heard in open court.

sentences.speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
sentences.text: This is in line with the overall confidential nature of such arbitral proceedings and will result in cost and time savings for parties who now do not have to apply for such proceedings to be heard in private.

sentences.speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
sentences.text: This Bill is the culmination of years of effort to re-design our Court system to enable it to be future-ready and well-equipped to meet the evolving needs of society.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
sentences.text: The Workers' Party supports the Bill and the majority of the proposed amendments such as the ones related to supporting the digital transformation of the Judiciary, the simplification of court terminology, civil justice reforms and the empowerment of the High Court to grant interim relief in aid of foreign court proceedings.

sections.label: Court not examining AG's grounds
sections.summary: The Court is not to examine the merits of the Attorney-General's public interest grounds for intervention before granting permission.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
sentences.text: A critical element of the proposed amendments is that the Court is not to examine the merits of the AG's grounds for intervention – essentially, the public interest grounds – before granting permission.

sections.label: Court cannot examine AG's merits
sections.summary: The Court may consider stage of proceedings and prejudice to parties but cannot examine the merits of the Attorney-General's public interest grounds.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
sentences.text: But while the Court may consider matters such as the stage the proceedings have reached, prejudice to the parties, yet again, the Court cannot examine the merits of the AG's grounds as to the public interest the AG is protecting.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
sentences.text: This onus placed on parties reverses the usual order of things in Court and the common law position on the AG's right to intervene where it is the party who wants something who should apply for it and justify it.

sections.label: Attorney-General intervention amendments and Australia
sections.summary: The Government seeks to replace the Court's role in deciding intervention merits, citing Australia's common law and statutory AG intervention rights.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
sentences.text: The Government now seeks to replace the Court's function of deciding on the merits of an application to intervene with the proposed amendments to the Attorney-General (Additional Functions) Act that are before the House.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
sentences.text: In Australia, at common law, the AG has the right to intervene in cases affecting the prerogatives of the Crown.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
sentences.text: This right has been extended by statute to cases involving, for example, the interpretation of the Constitution and the Migration Act.

sections.label: Canada Attorney-General intervention rules
sections.summary: In Canada the AG can intervene in constitutional matters without leave but must apply for leave on non-constitutional matters.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
sentences.text: In Canada, the AG can intervene in constitutional matters without obtaining leave but on non-constitutional matters, the AG must apply for leave.

sections.label: Singapore civil cases intervention question
sections.summary: It asks whether recent Singapore civil cases exist where the Government wished to intervene without the Court examining the Attorney-General's public interest grounds.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
sentences.text: Have there been civil cases in Singapore recently that the Government wishes it could have intervened in without having the Court examine the merits of the grounds for the Attorney-General's opinion as to the public interest under the proposed amendments?

sections.label: New public interest areas and COVID-19
sections.summary: It asks whether new public interest areas have arisen, and notes COVID-19 hastened digital transformation of Singapore's justice administration.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
sentences.text: More generally and as an extension of the above two questions: are there new areas of public interest that have hitherto not come up, which the Government is trying to protect?

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
sentences.text: On the first point, one silver lining to the COVID-19 pandemic is that it has hastened the digital transformation of the administration of justice in Singapore.

sections.label: Remote hearings and litigants-in-persons
sections.summary: The speaker supports a permanent framework for remote or paper hearings but worries litigants-in-persons lacking technology or writing access may be disadvantaged.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
sentences.text: For these reasons, I fully support the move to enact a permanent framework that will empower the Court to conduct remote hearings or even paper hearings.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
sentences.text: One concern I have though is how to ensure that litigants-in-persons (LIPs) who may not be familiar with or do not have access to video conferencing technology or have concerns about expressing themselves in writing are not disadvantaged by remote or paper hearings.

sections.label: Privileged accused-counsel remote conversations
sections.summary: It asks how conversations between accused persons in prisons and their counsel joining remotely will be kept strictly privileged and confidential.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
sentences.text: How is it being proposed that conversations between the accused persons in prisons and their counsel joining in from another location in the course of remote proceedings will be kept strictly privileged and confidential?

sections.label: AG intervention court discretion
sections.summary: Asks whether the Court retains discretion to weigh all relevant factors before allowing the Attorney-General's intervention.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
sentences.text: My next question is whether it is intended that when a Court decides that it is necessary for the AG to intervene, it would still have a discretion to consider all factors which are relevant to the balance of justice in the particular case, before it makes its decision whether or not to allow the intervention.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
sentences.text: This is the power that is provided for with the Courts under the Rules of Court when hearing the usual joinder applications.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
sentences.text: I seek the hon Minister's clarification as to whether it is intended that the same approach will apply to the AG.

sections.label: Justice administration moral imperatives
sections.summary: States two moral imperatives: administration of justice must not disadvantage any group, and the AG's power must derive from the Constitution.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
sentences.text: The first relates to a key moral imperative, that in the administration of justice, the means of administration must not disadvantage any group.

sentences.speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
sentences.text: My second point is also a moral imperative, that in the administration of justice, the source of power for the guardian of public interest, the hon AG, must derive, not just from common law, but from the highest law of the land, our Constitution.

sections.label: Court-ordered amicable resolution
sections.summary: Rules let the Court consider parties' alternative dispute-resolution conduct in costs orders, and new paragraph 23 lets the Court order amicable resolution attempts.

sentences.speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: The Rules allow the Court to consider how parties acted during their attempts at alternative dispute-resolution when making its decision on costs orders.

sentences.speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: However, with the new paragraph 23 of the First Schedule of the Supreme Court of Judicature Act, the Court can now order parties to attempt an amicable resolution.

sections.label: Immunity for Court mediators
sections.summary: New section 79 gives legal immunity to Court registrars and Court-appointed mediators for actions taken in mediation or alternative dispute resolution.

sentences.speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: My second clarification is on the new section 79, which gives legal immunity to the Court registrars and Court-appointed mediators for actions that they take as part of mediation or alternative dispute resolution for the Supreme Court.

sections.label: Mediation training for registrars
sections.summary: Asks whether Registrars, Deputy Registrars and Assistant Registrars must undergo mediation and alternative resolution training given extended immunity.

sentences.speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: With the extension of immunity to officers in the Supreme Court, will the Registrar, Deputy Registrars and Assistant Registrars be required to undergo training in mediation and other alternative resolution processes?

sections.label: Video link hearing protocol
sections.summary: Asks whether the Court will consider a protocol to standardise how live video link hearings are conducted.

sentences.speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: Will the Court consider implementing a protocol for proceedings conducted by way of a live video link to standardise the way video link hearings are conducted?

sections.label: Penalty for making recordings
sections.summary: Anyone who makes such recordings is penalised, even if not the source or present in Court.

sentences.speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: Anyone who makes such recordings, even if they were not the source of the original recording or was present in Court at the time, would be penalised.

sections.label: Foreign expert witnesses video link
sections.summary: Expert witnesses from other countries can give testimony by live video link without coming to Singapore.

sentences.speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: Expert witnesses from other countries can now provide testimony through live video link without having to come to Singapore.

sections.label: AG intervention in proceedings
sections.summary: Paragraph 10 amends the Attorney-General (Additional Functions) Act to let the AG intervene in any proceedings, retrospectively, in the public interest.

sentences.speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: Lastly, paragraph 10 introduces amendments to the Attorney-General (Additional Functions) Act, which enable the AG to intervene in any proceedings, even those that are not criminal proceedings, to which the AG is neither a party nor representing a party and retrospectively, in the public interest.

sections.label: AG deemed party after intervention
sections.summary: Under new section 4A(9), once granted permission to intervene, the AG is deemed a party with the same right of appeal.

sentences.speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: For example, under the new section 4A(9), once the AG is granted permission by the Courts to intervene in any proceedings, he is deemed a party to the proceedings and inter alia, has the same right of appeal in the proceedings.

sections.label: Subpoena renamed order to attend
sections.summary: An example of simplification is changing the expression of subpoena to an order to attend court.

sentences.speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
sentences.text: An example of such simplification is changing the expression of "subpoena" to "an order to attend court".

sections.label: Remote hearings formally legislated
sections.summary: The amendments formally legislate the practice of remote hearings.

sentences.speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
sentences.text: The amendments formally legislate the practice of remote hearings.

sections.label: Disruptive technologies judicial safeguards
sections.summary: Asks how robust current technical safeguards in the judicial system are against rapidly evolving disruptive technologies.

sentences.speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
sentences.text: Considering the rapidly evolving forms of such disruptive technologies, how robust are the current technical safeguards within our judicial system in countering such threats?

sections.label: Court intention amicable resolution
sections.summary: Asks whether the Court should consider parties' intention when ordering them to attempt amicable resolution.

sentences.speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
sentences.text: It also prevents Singapore from becoming increasingly litigious.

sentences.speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
sentences.text: However, I would like to clarify if the Court should consider the intention of parties in exercising its powers to order parties to attempt to resolve disputes by amicable resolution.

sections.label: Courts Reform Bill technology flexibility
sections.summary: States the Courts Reform Bill empowers Courts to conduct proceedings more flexibly using technology.

sentences.speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
sentences.text: One of the major components of this Courts Reform Bill is set to empower the Courts to conduct proceedings more flexibly by leveraging on the use of technology.

sections.label: Remote working new norm
sections.summary: States the reform Bill reaffirms remote working as part of the new norm.

sentences.speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
sentences.text: Another of my peers also remarked that remote working has provided him with more opportunities to spend more quality time and attend to the needs of his aged parents.

sentences.speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
sentences.text: This reform Bill reaffirms remote working as part of the new norm.

sections.label: E-Litigation virtual Court platform
sections.summary: Proposes tapping GovTech expertise to improve E-Litigation or create a virtual Court platform with chat, queue and SMS alerts.

sentences.speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
sentences.text: In this regard, I would like to propose whether the Ministry can facilitate, after taking into account the feedback of users from the Courts as well as members of the Bar, to tap on the expertise of GovtTech in improving the features of the E-Litigation system or creating a new virtual Court platform that is equipped with an integrated chat function and a dynamic queue system.

sentences.speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
sentences.text: With an SMS alert system for the queue, users can manage their waiting time more effectively and efficiently.

sections.label: Assistance for small law firms
sections.summary: Asks if the Ministry can offer assistance schemes for small law firms to buy equipment and if Courts can provide more spaces.

sentences.speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
sentences.text: In light of the disadvantages faced by lawyers practising in sole proprietorships or small partnerships, I would like to ask if the Ministry can look into offering some assistance schemes that enable the affected law firms to purchase the necessary equipment to attend such virtual hearings and whether the Courts can provide more spaces that will allow small law firm practitioners to communicate with their clients in person whilst adhering to safe distancing measures.

sections.label: Help for smaller law firms
sections.summary: A Member asks whether the Ministry will help smaller law firms access equipment through existing schemes, and suggests reviewing court filing and hearing fees.

sentences.speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
sentences.text: In this context, would the Ministry be looking into more ways to help these smaller law firms gain access to the equipment or “hardware” with the aid of these same schemes, so that they can fully transition into the digital era without transferring the cost of such implementation on their clients?

sentences.speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
sentences.text: (In Mandarin):   To many, litigation is a costly and time-consuming process.

sentences.speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
sentences.text: I support the recommendations made in this reform Bill, such as simplifying Court terminology across our statute books, to ensure that our laws are accessible to the public and easy to understand; as well as leveraging on technology for Court process with a view to reducing the costs of litigation.

sentences.speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
sentences.text: Apart from that, I hope the Ministry can further consider reviewing and reducing the Court filing and hearing fees.

sections.label: Simplifying court language and digitalisation
sections.summary: The amendments make legal proceedings more accessible by simplifying court language and support digital transformation plans for an efficient legal system.

sentences.speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
sentences.text: The amendments will enable legal proceedings to be more accessible to everyone by simplifying the language used in Court and support our overall digital transformation plans, keeping our legal system efficient and ready to meet the evolving needs of society in the future.

sections.label: Miranda warning versus Singapore system
sections.summary: The Miranda warning is used in the American system, while in Singapore's legal system remaining silent could draw adverse inferences.

sentences.speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
sentences.text: The Miranda warning, for example, is used in the American system, where a citizen's right to remain silent is read to the person being arrested.

sentences.speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
sentences.text: However, in our legal system, remaining silent could draw adverse inferences.

sections.label: Remote sentencing of Punithan Genasan
sections.summary: The remote sentencing of Punithan Genasan by Zoom in May 2020 was understandable during the COVID-19 pandemic, and the Member supports the Bill.

sentences.speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
sentences.text: As an example, the remote sentencing of Punithan Genasan where he was handed the death penalty via Zoom in May 2020 was understandable at the height of the COVID-19 pandemic.

sentences.speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
sentences.text: Notwithstanding the clarifications above, Sir, I support the Bill.

sections.label: Private consultations during remote hearings
sections.summary: During remote hearings, SPS facilitates private consultations between accused persons and lawyers by telephone, Zoom breakout room or separate cubicle.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
sentences.text: In the course of a remote hearing, over Zoom or tele-presence, SPS will facilitate the private consultation sessions between accused persons and their lawyers.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
sentences.text: These can be done through the telephone, a virtual breakout room on Zoom or a separate cubicle with a Zoom session between the accused person and his lawyer.

sections.label: One-stop platform for lawyers
sections.summary: A one-stop platform will help lawyers access key functions from solutions and systems, introduced in phases from the first quarter of 2022.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
sentences.text: This platform will be a one-stop shop to help lawyers access key functions from such solutions and systems more seamlessly.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
sentences.text: We aim to introduce the platform to the industry in phases, starting from the first quarter of 2022.

sections.label: COVID-19 SME funding exception
sections.summary: An exception was made last year due to COVID-19, providing 80% funding support for all SMEs, including law firms, to procure laptops and commonly used software.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
sentences.text: But we made an exception last year because of COVID-19.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
sentences.text: We worked to provide 80% funding support for all SMEs, including law firms, to procure laptops and commonly used software, such as Microsoft Office.

sections.label: Accused's right to be heard
sections.summary: The use of paper or asynchronous hearings must not undermine the accused's right to be heard, and this Bill protects that right.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
sentences.text: So, we have to make sure the use of paper or asynchronous hearings do not undermine the accused's right to be heard.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
sentences.text: This Bill protects the accused's right to be heard.

sections.label: Recording physical Court proceedings
sections.summary: Recording physical Court proceedings is already contempt of the Court.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
sentences.text: Today, it is already contempt of the Court to record physical Court proceedings.

sections.label: Court Volunteer Mediator requirements
sections.summary: Court Volunteer Mediators must minimally be an Associate Mediator with the Singapore Mediation Centre with at least three years of mediation experience.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
sentences.text: As for Court Volunteer Mediators, they must minimally be an Associate Mediator with the Singapore Mediation Centre with at least three years of mediation experience.

sections.label: No plans for Supreme Court
sections.summary: Given the nature of disputes and value of claims filed in the Supreme Court, there are no immediate plans to do so.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
sentences.text: Given the nature of the disputes and the value of the claims filed in the Supreme Court, there are no immediate plans to do so.

sections.label: Joinder to SICC proceedings
sections.summary: A party can be joined to existing SICC proceedings without consent, just as with the High Court or State Courts.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
sentences.text: Mr Zhulkarnain also pointed out the joinder of a non-consenting party to SICC proceedings, and spoke about the enforcement of an SICC judgment in a foreign jurisdiction.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
sentences.text: It is possible for a party to be joined to existing proceedings before SICC without that party's consent; just like it is possible for a party to be joined to existing proceedings before the High Court or the State Courts without that party's consent.

sections.label: Enforcing SICC judgments
sections.summary: Enforcement of an SICC judgment against a party properly served but not submitting to jurisdiction will be similar to enforcement of a High Court General Division judgment.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
sentences.text: With regard to enforcement, the enforcement of a SICC judgment against a party, who has been properly served, but has not submitted to SICC's jurisdiction, will be similar to the enforcement of a judgment issued by the General Division of the High Court against a party that has not submitted to the jurisdiction of the General Division.

sections.label: AG intervention on negligence test
sections.summary: The AG intervened on the applicable legal test for negligence in the provision of medical advice in Hii Chii Kok v Ooi Peng Jin.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
sentences.text: For example, the AG has intervened on the applicable legal test for negligence in relation to the provision of medical advice, in the case of Hii Chii Kok v Ooi Peng Jin, between two parties.

sections.label: Courts decide validity of arguments
sections.summary: The amendments provide for the AG's right to intervene, but the Courts ultimately decide the merits of the substantive case.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
sentences.text: Ultimately, of course, it is up to the Courts to decide on the validity of the arguments.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
sentences.text: So, the amendments provide for the right of the AG to intervene for that purpose but, ultimately, the Court decides on the merits of the substantive case.

sections.label: Court of Appeal on AG intervention
sections.summary: The Court of Appeal allowed the AG to intervene, affirmed his position as Guardian of public interest, and held non-intervention would be dereliction of public duty.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
sentences.text: The Court of Appeal allowed the AG to intervene, affirmed the AG's position as Guardian of public interest and it further held that if the AG does not intervene despite taking the view that there are issues of the public interest, then the AG would, in fact, be in dereliction of his public duty.

sections.label: Statutory framework for AG intervention
sections.summary: The AG intervenes to protect the common man, and a clear statutory framework is being enacted for the AG's right to intervene.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
sentences.text: The AG is intervening to protect the man in the street – the common man.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
sentences.text: We are moving to enact a clear statutory framework for the AG's right to intervene, to lend certainty to this area of law, so that parties can proceed expeditiously to the substantive issues in the case.

sections.label: Studying constitutionalising AG's role
sections.summary: The Ministry will study whether to put the AG's established role in the Constitution, taking into account how the law and jurisprudence develop.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
sentences.text: My Ministry will study this suggestion whether we should put it in the Constitution the AG's established role in this respect, taking into account how this area of law and the jurisprudence develop.

sections.label: AG intervention procedure amendments
sections.summary: The amendments state on their face that they clarify the Attorney-General's intervention procedure and reduce satellite litigation and delays.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
sentences.text: The short answer is, the amendments say what they say on the face of it.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
sentences.text: They are meant to lend clarity to the procedure for the AG to intervene and to minimise satellite litigation and delays.

sections.label: AG duty to disclose grounds
sections.summary: The Attorney-General must properly disclose his grounds for intervention to the Court, and the Courts ultimately decide by discretion.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
sentences.text: The AG will have a duty to disclose properly his grounds for intervention to the Court.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
sentences.text: The Courts, generally, understand that the AG does not act frivolously, vexatiously or egregiously in pursuing the public interest, but, ultimately, it is a matter of discretion for the Courts.

sections.label: New Rules definitions list
sections.summary: The new rules of Court will contain a clear list of definitions upfront.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
sentences.text: The new rules of Court will contain a clear list of definitions upfront.

sections.label: Terminology changes with revamp
sections.summary: The terminology changes will be effected with the revamp, and most are aligned with other Courts.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
sentences.text: The terminology changes will be effected with the revamp and the majority of which are aligned with other Courts.

sections.label: Standard ex parte application process
sections.summary: What is being done is nothing new and is the standard process for an ex parte application.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: Just to be clear, what is being done is nothing new.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: It is the standard process when there is an ex parte application.

sections.label: AG as guardian of public interest
sections.summary: The speaker suggests Courts address substantive arguments earlier, since the Attorney-General is a senior Legal Officer and Guardian of the public interest.

sentences.speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
sentences.text: I am suggesting that, in view of the earlier point I made about costs, if the Courts can look into the substantive arguments later on, why not just allow them to do so earlier?

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: I think this simply takes from the principle, Mr Singh, and Members will accept, really, that the AG is a senior Legal Officer, the Guardian of the public interest.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: If he says that, "I am saying this as a matter of public interest", we do not want an extended argument, trying to delay proceedings by the parties, by saying whether there is or there is no public interest.

sections.label: Court application decision
sections.summary: The matter can be taken up with the Courts, which will decide after an application is made.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: As I have said, this is a matter that can be taken up with the Courts.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: Make the application and then they will have to make a decision.

sections.label: Amendment reasons and responses
sections.summary: Minister Edwin Tong explained the amendment reasons yesterday, and the speaker decided to respond to Members' questions, including Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: The reasons for the amendments have been explained in the speech by Minister Edwin Tong yesterday.

sentences.speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
sentences.text: A number of Members have raised questions and even if they did not speak, I have decided to respond, like Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim.
